name: csmith
desc: Generates random C programs conforming to the C99 standard
why: Generates random valid C programs to find compiler bugs, a strange and genuinely clever way to stress-test toolchains.

brief.what_it_is: Csmith is a random generator of C programs. You run the csmith command, optionally with options, and it writes one randomly generated C program to standard output, which you redirect to a .c file. The README says the output is free of undefined behaviors and also produces statistics about each generated program. The generated programs are meant to be compiled and run, and their output compared across compilers.
brief.why_it_exists: The primary purpose is to find compiler bugs with random programs, using differential testing as the test oracle. The README also says it can serve anyone who needs a test suite of C programs and doesn't want to write them by hand.
brief.how_it_works: Csmith generates a random C program for each run. You compile that program with two or more compilers (for example gcc and clang), run both binaries, and compare their outputs. Any difference points to a bug in one compiler, or in the unlikely case, in Csmith itself. The README says to repeat this in scripts to amplify the testing and to apply timeouts, since generated programs might contain infinite loops.

brief.install_notes: The README gives source build steps for Ubuntu: install g++, cmake and m4, then cmake, make and make install. Tarball downloads are listed as coming soon. Windows builds have a separate guide in doc/build-csmith-on-windows.md. The brew metadata (not the README) recommends setting the environment variable CSMITH_PATH to $HOMEBREW_CELLAR/csmith/2.3.0/include/csmith-2.3.0. Compiled test programs need the Csmith include directory on the compiler's include path, as the examples show with -I. Installed executables are csmith, compiler_test.pl and launchn.pl.
brief.standout: Instead of checking a program against an expected answer, it generates valid C programs that avoid undefined behavior and uses disagreement between compilers as the bug signal. The README notes that producing UB-free programs is not trivial, and that the project was built as research on finding bugs in C compilers.
brief.status: Quiet, with evidence from the README only. It says the project is maintained on the authors' discretionary time and that responses to bug reports or feature requests might be delayed. The fetched page showed no release date or last commit date, so I could not confirm recent activity. The brew description is a single line.
brief.caveats: The README's install steps are written for Ubuntu. Tarball releases are marked coming soon. The generated programs can contain infinite loops, so timeouts are needed. Responses to issues may be slow. Windows building needs a separate guide. The README does not say what license applies.

entry.title: Csmith
entry.tldr: Csmith writes random C programs that avoid undefined behavior, so you can compile them with different compilers and treat any disagreement as a bug.
entry.deeper_look:
Run `csmith` and it prints one randomly generated C program to standard output. Redirect it to a file, compile it, run it. The program computes something opaque and prints a result. That result is not interesting on its own. It becomes interesting when you compile the same file with a second compiler and the two binaries disagree.

That is differential testing, and it is the idea underneath the tool. There is no expected answer to check against. If gcc and clang are both correct and the program is well defined, they must produce the same output. A mismatch points to a bug in one compiler, or, as the README puts it, in the unlikely case, in Csmith itself.

The hard part is the guarantee. In the README's words, Csmith outputs C programs free of undefined behaviors ("believe us, that's not trivial"). Without that, a mismatch could just mean the program was allowed to do anything. The project was built as research on finding bugs in C compilers, and the PLDI 2011 paper linked below describes the work.

The README also suggests it for anyone who needs a pile of C test programs and does not want to write them by hand. The package installs two Perl scripts alongside `csmith`, `compiler_test.pl` and `launchn.pl`, though the brief does not describe what they do.
entry.install:
brew install csmith
# Brew recommends setting CSMITH_PATH:
export CSMITH_PATH=$HOMEBREW_CELLAR/csmith/2.3.0/include/csmith-2.3.0
# Compiling generated programs needs a C compiler (gcc or clang) and Csmith's include directory on the include path via -I.

try_this.what_happens: Generates one random C program and writes it to random1.c.
Compiles the generated program with gcc, using Csmith's include directory. Adjust the -I path to wherever your install keeps its headers.
Lists the command line options for customizing what gets generated.

entry.whats_unique: It needs no expected answers. It generates valid C that avoids undefined behavior and uses disagreement between compilers as the bug signal.
entry.caveats: The README says the project is maintained on the authors' discretionary time and replies may be slow. Generated programs can loop forever, so run them under a timeout.
